blocks.text: Many bacteria can survive extended periods of harsh conditions by forming specialised "resting" cells called endospores. Endospores are thick-walled and metabolically inactive, that is, dormant. The process by which a bacterium makes an endospore is called sporulation.

blocks.title: Endospore and sporulation
blocks.text: An endospore is a thick-walled, dormant resting cell formed inside a bacterium so that it can withstand unfavourable conditions. Sporulation is the process of forming it. Sporulation is a survival mechanism, not a way of reproducing: one cell gives one endospore.

items: When a bacterium faces unfavourable conditions, it replicates its DNA.
The cell membrane makes a septum that isolates the new DNA together with a small portion of cytoplasm.
The cell membrane grows again around the new DNA, the cytoplasm and the septum, so the new DNA is now surrounded by two membranes.
The DNA of the vegetative (parent) cell disintegrates and the whole cell begins to dehydrate.
A new peptidoglycan layer forms between the two membranes around the separated DNA and cytoplasm, and a spore coat forms around it.
The structure matures into an endospore. The vegetative cell breaks and the endospore is released.

blocks.alt: Six stages drawn left to right: a rod cell replicates its DNA; a septum walls off one copy; the membrane wraps the copy in a second membrane; the parent DNA breaks down; peptidoglycan and a spore coat form around the forespore; the parent cell breaks open and the endospore is released.
blocks.caption: Endospore formation (sporulation) in a bacterium (original diagram after Figure 2.4).
blocks.long_description: Stage 1 shows a rod-shaped cell with two copies of its circular DNA. Stage 2 adds a septum near one end, enclosing one copy with a little cytoplasm. Stage 3 shows the membrane engulfing that compartment so it is double-membraned (the forespore). Stage 4 shows the parent's DNA fading and the cell shrinking as it dehydrates. Stage 5 shows a thick peptidoglycan layer and a dark spore coat around the forespore. Stage 6 shows the parent cell's wall broken and the oval endospore free.

blocks.text: The endospore remains dormant unless favourable conditions return. When they do, the endospore germinates and gives rise to a new vegetative cell.

blocks.title: Why the spore survives
blocks.text: Two membranes, a fresh peptidoglycan layer and a spore coat shield the DNA, and dehydration halts metabolism. That is why endospores withstand heat, drying and other harsh conditions that would kill the vegetative cell.

blocks.prompt: Put the events of sporulation in order: spore coat forms; DNA replicates; septum isolates one DNA copy; endospore released; parent DNA disintegrates and cell dehydrates; second membrane surrounds the new DNA.
blocks.explanation: DNA replicates; a septum isolates one copy with some cytoplasm; the membrane grows round it, giving two membranes; the parent DNA disintegrates and the cell dehydrates; peptidoglycan and a spore coat form; the endospore matures and is released when the parent cell breaks.

items: Endospores are thick-walled, dormant resting cells that let bacteria survive harsh conditions.

Sporulation: DNA replicates, a septum isolates one copy, a second membrane wraps it, the parent DNA disintegrates and the cell dehydrates, peptidoglycan and a spore coat form, the endospore matures and is released.
The endospore germinates into a new vegetative cell when favourable conditions return.
